Plasmid transfection was accomplished with Lipofectamine 2000 according to manufacturer’s protocols (Invitrogen).

#### Generation of ALC1 knockout cell lines

CRISPR-Cas9 plasmids (pSpCas9(BB)–2A-Puro (PX459) v2.0; Addgene plasmid #: 62988) targeting the ALC1 gene (for gRNA targeting sequences, see Supplementary file 10) were transfected into HEK293T cells. Targeting sequences were obtained using the Genetic Perturbation Platform (Broad Institute). After 24 h, 2 μg/mL of puromycin (Sigma) was added to growth medium and cells were selected for 48 hr. Puromycin was then removed, dead cells were washed away, and the adhering live cells were left to recover for 24 h prior to dilution for single colony selection. Clones were screened via western blot for ALC1 and those with no detectable ALC1 were frozen down and stored in liquid nitrogen.

### Nuclear extract preparation

Nuclear extract was prepared as previously described (Carey et al., 2009) with some modifications. The cells were dounced with a B-type pestle (Kontle Glass Co) until they were lysed. Lysis was confirmed by staining with Trypan Blue dye and visualizing under a microscope. The cell number was estimated using a hemocytometer and the volumes of the different buffers were added depending on that. The nuclear lysate was homogenized using pestle B until it was properly resuspended in Buffer C. The crude nuclear lysate was dialyzed into Buffer D in a dialysis tubing (FisherScientific, 6–8 kDa MWCO) at 4 °C, and dialysis was stopped before first signs of precipitation (around 3–4 h).

### Nuclear extract nucleosome remodeling assay

Nucleosome remodeling reactions (25 μL) were carried out in REA Buffer with 1 μL of PstI (NEB, at 100,000 U/mL), 2 mM ATP, and 8 μL of nuclear extract derived from either wild-type or ALC1 knockout HEK293T cells and 20 nM of the desired nucleosome substrate. The reactions were carried out at 30 °C and quenched with Quench Buffer at 0 min and 60 min time points. We note that reactions contain 0.5 mM DTT (carried over from the lysate storage buffer). The 601 DNA was isolated as described in ‘Restriction enzyme accessibility-based nucleosome remodeling assay’ section and analyzed on a 5% TBE gel. Western blot analyses of the ADPr profile of each nucleosome employed in this assay were carried out after incubation with or without either nuclear extract under identical reaction conditions.

### Preparation of H3S10/H3S28ADPr4-modified C-terminal SEA peptide

The tetra-ADP-ribosylated species of H3 (1–20) thioester and H3 (21–34, N-terminal thiazolidine, C-terminal SEA) peptides were purified to homogeneity using RP-HPLC and lyophilized. The tetra-ADP-ribosylated H3 (21–34) SEA peptide was resuspended in a degassed buffer containing 6 M guanidine hydrochloride, 0.1 M sodium phosphate pH 8.0% and 5% DMSO to a concentration of 1 mM. This reaction was rotated at room temperature for 16 h and SEA ring oxidation was confirmed by a –2 Da mass change via LC-MS. A stock of 1 M O-Methylhydroxylamine HCl (Combi-Blocks) was prepared in a degassed buffer containing 6 M guanidine hydrochloride and 0.1 M sodium phosphate pH 4.0, and added to the reaction to a final concentration of 200 mM. The pH of the reaction was adjusted to 4.0 and the reaction incubated at 37 °C for 2 h. Deprotection of the thiazolidine ring was confirmed by a –12 Da mass shift via LC-MS. The tetra-ADP-ribosylated H3 (1–20) thioester peptide was resuspended in a degassed buffer containing 6 M guanidine hydrochloride and 0.1 M sodium phosphate pH 7.0 to a concentration of 1 mM and a volume equal to that of the above reaction. The two peptide solutions were combined and 2,2,2-trifluoroethanethiol (Sigma-Aldrich) was added to a final concentration of 150 mM. The pH of this reaction was then adjusted to 7.0 and it was incubated at 37 °C for 16 h. The ligation product was purified over semi-preparative RP-HPLC and lyophilized. This product was resuspended in a buffer containing 6 M guanidine hydrochloride and 0.1 M sodium phosphate pH 7.0, and TCEP was added to it to a final concentration of 20 mM. The ligated product with a reduced, C-terminal SEA ring was confirmed by a single peak on RP-HPLC and a single mass on LC-MS. For synthetic scheme and characterization, see Supplementary file 9.

Reviewer #1 (Recommendations for the authors):

Histone modifications play diverse roles in regulating DNA based transactions. Understanding the biochemical mechanisms underlying such roles has been greatly enabled by the ability to reconstitute chromatin templates with defined modifications. Poly-ADP-ribosylation (poly-ADPr) is a major modification that plays critical roles in DNA damage. However a few features have slowed careful mechanistic dissection of the role of poly-ADP-ribosylation. These features include that (i) the modification is found on multiple proteins such as histones and the PARP enzymes that deposit the modification and (ii) there is heterogeneity in terms of the poly-ADP-ribosylation chain length and the amino-acid location of the modification. Additionally, unlike with other histone modifications such as acetylation, methylation and ubiquitylation, generating homogenously modified poly-ADPr chromatin in vitro has been technically challenging. Here the authors generate nucleosomes with homogenously and site-specifically modified poly-ADPr marks through a series of readily separable steps. Using these modified nucleosomes the authors test the impact of the poly-ADPr modifications on the activity of the chromatin remodeler ALC1. Previous work has shown that ALC1 is activated by binding poly-ADPr chains that have 3+ units. However, it has not been clear which modified substrates are being recognized by ALC1. Using their site-specifically modified reagents the authors show clearly that poly-ADP-ribosylation of H2A (and H3) has a much larger effect on stimulating nucleosome remodeling than auto-ADP-ribosylated PARP.

Overall, the work in this resource article is carefully carried out with several thoughtful controls and provides a highly enabling new method for the chromatin field. What further raises the impact of this work is the use of this new method to make a significant new mechanistic finding about ALC1regulation. I think the work in this resource article will be of much interest to the chromatin community and those studying DNA damage.

Reviewer #2 (Recommendations for the authors):

This interesting manuscript from Liszczak and coworkers highlights the strength of a semisynthetic chemical approach to obtain both monomeric and well-defined polymeric ADP-ribosylated histones H2B and H3. The authors have applied these reagents toward dissecting the role of ADP-ribose in facilitating nucleosome remodeling by the macrodomain-containing remodeler ALC1. Unfortunately, the synthetic novelty is somewhat diminished by a very recent manuscript from Muir and coworkers in JACS reporting the semisynthesis of identical mono-ADP-ribosylated H2B and H3. However, the current manuscript focuses on biochemical roles of ADP-ribosylation that were not addressed by Muir, and also presents the elegant enzymatic extension of semisynthetic mono-ADP ribosylated histones to obtain well-defined polymers of ADP-ribose by using varying ratios of PARP1:HPF1. The rigorous series of experiments and interesting results, that begin to clarify prior hypotheses generated from cellular data, will be of broad interest to the readers of eLife. I recommend a few figure/text revisions and the inclusion of two additional experiments, with the reagents on hand, to help increase the clarity of techniques and conclusions presented.

One key limitation of the work – which the authors clearly state in the methods for assembly of full-length ADP-ribosylated histones – is the requirement for a Cys-containing mutant H2B and H3 in biochemical assays. While there is no doubt, given Muir's recent work and the authors' claims, that the Cys may be effectively desulfurized in future experiments, the current substrates tested did not include this step. Therefore, I would suggest the authors move their statement on desulfurization to the Results in the main text and cite the Muir JACS paper. Accordingly, Figure 4A should clearly show the thiol is present in the histone tail. Finally, given the risk of disulfide-tethering cysteine-containing proteins to this accessible thiol in the H2B/H3 tail, the authors should mention in the discussion if reducing agents were included for all enzymatic assays and whether assay products were analyzed to ensure Cys-containing H2B/H3 remained as monomeric species at the end of the assay period. Particularly when mononucleosomes were subjected to nuclear lysates in remodeling assays.

In Figure 4. It is surprising that H3 and H2B appear to migrate at the same size prior to ADP-ribosylation despite previous reports of their differing migration (see https://www.epicypher.com/products/nucleosomes/histone-octamer-recombinant-human for one example). The authors should indicate the percentage of polyacrylamide or any changes in gel running conditions from standard SDS-PAGE conditions that led to this result.

Supplementary Figure 5F. The PARP1-SerADPlong size clearly changes with hydroxylamine treatment (comparing lanes 3 and 4) indicating that a minority of ADP-ribose linkages are not to Ser in PARP1. I would suggest noting this in the main text as potential heterogeneity in the ADP-ribosylated protein being employed in assays. Particularly if the ADP-ribosylated PARP1 tested in biochemical assays was not first treated with hydroxylamine.

Two important biochemical assays are missing in the manuscript that would help readers understand the specific contributions of nucleosome ADP-ribosylation and PARP1 ADP-ribosylation toward remodeling by ALC1.

(A) The first assay is to investigate competition of ADP-ribosylated nucleosomes by ADP-ribosylated peptides. This would validate the authors' statement that, "in addition to disrupting an autoinhibited conformation, the modified histone tail:macrodomain interaction is crucial for presenting the ATPase domain to the nucleosome." If this statement were indeed true and no additional nucleosomal contacts were needed for ALC1 function, then ADP-ribosylated H2B/H3 peptides would be expected to effectively inhibit nucleosome remodeling of the corresponding ADP-ribosylated nucleosome.

(B) The second assay involves an ALC1-mediated remodeling experiment with ADP-ribosylated nucleosomes in the presence of ADP-ribosylated PARP1. The authors, surprisingly, only test ADP-ribosylated PARP1 with unmodified nucleosomes and the rationale for this is unclear if DNA-damage is indeed accompanied by histone ADP-ribosylation, which is also the focus of this manuscript. Results from an assay with ADP-ribosylated H2B containing nucleosomes would clearly indicate if nucleosome ADP-ribosylation remains relevant when PARP1 is also ADP-ribosylated, and if any additive effects are observed from both species being ADP-ribosylated.

Finally, the pooled mononucleosome remodeling experiment provides no additional information beyond the initial information gained from individual mononucleosome assays and the fact that a ADP-ribosylated histone peptide does not activate ALC1 on non-ribosylated nucleosomes. The peptide in trans assay result already indicated that ALC1 does not stay active after disengaging the ADP-ribosylated peptide. If the authors' goal was to demonstrate that ribosylated nucleosomes do not stimulate activity of ALC1 on non-ribsoylated nucleosomes, or that ALC1 "immediately turns off" after disengagement from a ADP-ribosylated nucleosome, then this needs to be tested in an asymmetric dinucleosome model wherein the two nucleosomes are tethered in close proximity and not diffusing independently of each other. A mixture of varying ADP-ribosylated mononucleosomes at nM concentrations is unlikely to be an approximation of the chromatin context of ALC1, where varying degrees of ribosylation may exist in close apposition. Hence, I suggest the authors reword the conclusion from the pooled experiment to suggest that ALC1 only acts on polyADP-ribosylated mononucleosomes within a mixture of varying ADP-ribosylation states and avoid speculation of its diffusivity.

Reviewer #3 (Recommendations for the authors):

– While authors show that multiple modified histones can be made by this method (including S28 modified H3), claiming broad applicability to preparation of ADPr proteins is a misnomer for the exact reasons listed in the last paragraph of the discussion. The claims of broad applicability should be revised accordingly.

– Protein modification community would benefit from better understanding of pros and cons of the polyADP ribosylation method presented here. Given a need for extensive HPLC purification of the mixtures formed in both cases, a side-by-side comparison to experimentally simpler one pot reactions with PARP1:HPF1 would help.

– It would be important to assess whether ALC1 itself is ADP ribosylated in the remodeling assays where PARP is supplemented together with NAD+. The supplemental figure 5D, while showing PARP1 is autoribosylated based on the band shift, suggests broad ADP ribosylation signal as well. ALC1 autoribosylation might contribute to relief of its autoinhibition, contributing to the slight enhancement in remodeling observed, rather than a direct interaction with autoribosylated PARP1.

– Remodeling in nuclear extracts: The representative gel results in Figure 6 supplement 1C of remodeling in the presence of nuclear extracts does not support the claim that, with poly ADP ribosylated substrates, remodeling is enhanced compared to that observed with ALC1 knockout extracts. The relative remodeled and unremodeled bands appear similar regardless of the presence of ALC1 in the extract. It appears the specificity of remodeling gained for the ADPr4 substrate in the presence of ALC1 might result from slightly less remodeling of the unmodified substrate in the presence of ALC1 compared to ALC1 knockout extract unmodified substrate remodeling. This point would be apparent if the data was plotted as raw fraction remodeled values or relative remodeled values calculated to the unmodified substrate with WT extract for all experiments in Figure 6E.

– More rigorous characterization is needed for the poly ADP ribosylated substrates used with nuclear extracts in Figure 6E to support the claim that no hydrolysis is present of the poly ADP ribose chains. The band shifts due to poly ADP ribosylation are less pronounced as shown in Figure 4C-4E and the band shift is decreased upon addition of extract to H2BS6/H3S10ADPr4 substrate, suggesting chain hydrolysis. Authors should test if the polyADP ribose chains are retained after incubation with nuclear extracts. Alternatively, authors could test nuclear extract activity with and without ALC1 in the presence of PARG to assess if the enhancement is abolished.

– If it still holds, any speculation on attenuation of ALC1 stimulation in nuclear extracts, as opposed to that observed with recombinant components?

results.result: PARP1:HPF1 complex catalyzes serine-specific ADP-ribosylation on histone peptides, producing mono- and poly-ADP-ribosylated products with linear chain structures. H3S10 and H2BS6 are the sole acceptor residues on their respective peptides, as confirmed by mutagenesis and glycohydrolase treatment.
results.evaluation: Claims C18-C23 provide converging evidence from HPLC-MS, mutagenesis, and enzymatic digestion experiments. The characterization is thorough with appropriate controls (S10A/S6A mutants, PARG/ARH3 treatments) and LC-MS/MS analysis confirming linear chain structure with <0.03% branching.

results.result: HPF1 concentration modulates PARP1 activity from poly-ADP-ribosyltransferase to mono-ADP-ribosyltransferase. At 5 μM HPF1, ~41% mono-ADPr and ~59% poly-ADPr products are observed, while at 100 μM HPF1, ~94% mono-ADPr and ~6% di-ADPr are produced.
results.evaluation: Claims C24-C27 provide quantitative HPLC-based measurements with appropriate replication (n=3). The dose-response relationship is clear and the mechanistic interpretation (C28) is reasonable given the structural data cited. The quantification method using peak integration at A214/A280 with standardization curves is appropriate.

results.result: PARP1 and PARP2 efficiently elongate ADP-ribose chains from mono-ADP-ribosylated peptide substrates in the absence of HPF1, achieving ~70% conversion at 1 μM PARP1. HPF1 dose-dependently inhibits this elongation activity (IC50 ~14 μM), while the HPF1-D283A binding-deficient mutant shows no inhibition.
results.evaluation: Claims C29-C33 demonstrate a clear two-step enzymatic mechanism with appropriate controls (HPF1-D283A mutant). The quantitative measurements are consistent and the dose-response for HPF1 inhibition is well-characterized. The mutant control (C33) provides strong evidence for specificity.

results.result: A two-step enzymatic approach enables milligram-scale preparation of homogeneous poly-ADP-ribosylated peptides (up to tetra-ADPr) for multiple PARP1:HPF1 substrates including H2BS6, H3S10, TMA16-S9, PARP1-S507, and H3S28.
results.evaluation: Claims C34-C35 describe a scalable methodology with purification data shown in figures. The approach is validated across multiple substrates, demonstrating broad applicability. The milligram-scale yields are appropriate for downstream biochemical applications.

results.result: The ALC1 macrodomain binds tri-, tetra-, and penta-ADP-ribosylated H2B and H3 peptides with high affinity (Kd ~21-37 nM) but shows negligible binding to mono- and di-ADP-ribosylated species. Tri-ADPr is sufficient for optimal binding, and no sequence preference exists between H2BS6 and H3S10 sites.
results.evaluation: Claims C36-C40 present systematic fluorescence polarization data with appropriate controls (Af1521 macrodomain). The Kd values are well-determined with error bars (n=3). The conclusion about tri-ADPr sufficiency (C39) and lack of sequence preference (C40) are reasonable inferences from the similar affinities observed.

results.result: Six semi-synthetic full-length ADP-ribosylated histones (H2BS6ADPr1/3/4 and H3S10ADPr1/3/4) were prepared via native chemical ligation and characterized as >95% pure by HPLC/MS. These were assembled into eight unique histone octamers including doubly-modified species.
results.evaluation: Claims C41-C44 describe successful protein semi-synthesis with appropriate characterization (HPLC/MS, SDS-PAGE/western blot). The >95% purity threshold is appropriate for biochemical studies. The observation that ADPr chain length affects gel migration (C44) provides additional validation of sample homogeneity.

results.result: ALC1 exhibits low remodeling activity (<3×10⁻⁴ min⁻¹) on unmodified and mono-ADP-ribosylated nucleosomes but robust activity on tri- and tetra-ADP-ribosylated nucleosomes. The H2BS6/H3S10ADPr4 nucleosome increases ALC1 remodeling rate ~370-fold, with modest preference for H2BS6 site and tetra-ADPr chains.
results.evaluation: Claims C45-C48 present systematic remodeling kinetics with appropriate controls and replication. The ~370-fold stimulation is a striking quantitative result. Rate constants are determined by fitting to exponential decay models, which is appropriate for these assays. The data are consistent with the macrodomain binding results.

results.result: A macrodomain deletion construct of ALC1 (amino acids 1-673) shows no preference for H2BS6ADPr4 nucleosomes over unmodified nucleosomes, demonstrating that the macrodomain:histone tail interaction is critical for substrate selectivity.
results.evaluation: Claims C49-C50 provide a clear structure-function experiment. The deletion construct is an appropriate control that directly tests the role of the macrodomain. The loss of substrate preference in the deletion mutant strongly supports the mechanistic interpretation (C50).

results.result: Freely diffusing ADP-ribosylated peptides (H2BS6ADPr4 or H3S10ADPr4) cannot stimulate ALC1 remodeling of unmodified nucleosomes and do not inhibit nucleosome ADPr-dependent ALC1 activation, indicating that additional ALC1:nucleosome interfaces are required.
results.evaluation: Claims C51-C52 demonstrate that macrodomain engagement alone is insufficient for activation. The experiments test both stimulation and competition, providing complementary evidence. The interpretation that additional interfaces are required is reasonable and supported by cited structural studies.

results.result: Auto-ADP-ribosylated PARP1 stimulates ALC1 activity on unmodified nucleosomes (~12-fold for Asp/Glu-ADPr, ~28-36-fold for Ser-ADPr), but nucleosome serine ADPr is superior to PARP1 auto-ADPr for ALC1 activation in biochemical assays. Automodified PARP1 cannot further stimulate ALC1 when ADPr nucleosomes are used.
results.evaluation: Claims C53-C56 provide systematic comparison of different activation mechanisms with appropriate controls (hydroxylamine treatment to distinguish Ser vs Asp/Glu linkages). The quantitative fold-changes are well-determined. The caveat in C56 about not extrapolating to cellular context is appropriate scientific caution.

results.result: In competition assays with mixed nucleosome pools, ALC1 preferentially remodels binding-competent (tri- and tetra-ADP-ribosylated) nucleosome substrates, with modest preference for H2BS6ADPr4 over H2BS6ADPr3, consistent with single-substrate assays.
results.evaluation: Claims C57-C58 validate the single-substrate results using a more physiologically relevant competition format. The qPCR-based approach with unique primer pairs is technically sound. The consistency between competition and single-substrate assays strengthens confidence in the findings.

results.result: In asymmetric dinucleosomes, ALC1 preferentially remodels the ADP-ribosylated nucleosome (ADPrA-unmodB: ~79% remodeled) over the unmodified nucleosome adjacent to an ADP-ribosylated one (unmodA-ADPrB: ~21% remodeled), demonstrating that ALC1 rapidly returns to inactive conformation upon target disengagement.
results.evaluation: Claims C59-C61 provide elegant spatial control experiments. The asymmetric dinucleosome design directly tests whether ALC1 remains active after engaging one nucleosome. The large difference in remodeling efficiency (~79% vs ~21%) strongly supports the interpretation (C61) about rapid inactivation upon disengagement.

results.result: CHD4 remodels unmodified nucleosomes with rate constant ~0.01 min⁻¹, and this activity is not affected by nucleosome ADPr status, indicating that nucleosome serine ADPr specifically stimulates ALC1 rather than generally decreasing the energy barrier to DNA translocation.
results.evaluation: Claims C62-C63 provide an important specificity control. CHD4 shares 63% ATPase domain similarity with ALC1 but lacks a macrodomain, making it an appropriate control. The lack of ADPr-dependent stimulation for CHD4 strongly supports the specificity interpretation (C63).

results.result: Wild-type HEK293T nuclear extracts show ~3-fold increased remodeling activity toward H2BS6ADPr4 and H2BS6/H3S10ADPr4 nucleosomes but not H2BS6ADPr1 nucleosomes. ALC1-KO extracts show no substrate preference, confirming that ALC1 is responsible for ADPr-dependent remodeling in nuclear extracts.
results.evaluation: Claims C64-C66 demonstrate physiological relevance using nuclear extracts. The ALC1-KO control (C66) is critical and provides strong evidence that ALC1 is the primary ADPr-responsive remodeler in these extracts. The lack of response to mono-ADPr (C65) is consistent with all prior results.

results.result: HPF1 simultaneously stimulates mono-ADPr activity and blocks ADP-ribose chain elongation on trans-peptide substrates, supporting structural implications that mono- and poly-ADPr are mutually exclusive PARP1 activities.
results.evaluation: Claims C67-C68 synthesize the mechanistic findings from the HPLC-MS analyses. The interpretation (C68) appropriately integrates the biochemical data with cited structural studies (Suskiewicz et al., 2020). The conclusion about mutually exclusive activities is well-supported by the dose-response data.

results.result: A chemoenzymatic protein synthesis strategy was employed to assemble full-length ADP-ribosylated histones, demonstrating that ADPr at H2BS6 or H3S10 converts nucleosomes into robust ALC1 substrates.
results.evaluation: Claims C2-C3 summarize the overall technological and biological findings. The chemoenzymatic approach is validated through multiple lines of evidence (peptide synthesis, ligation, nucleosome assembly, functional assays). The conclusion about converting nucleosomes into ALC1 substrates is strongly supported by the remodeling data.

results.result: ALC1 preferentially remodels activated substrates within heterogeneous mononucleosome populations and asymmetrically ADP-ribosylated dinucleosomes, and nucleosome serine ADPr is sufficient to stimulate ALC1 activity in nuclear extracts.
results.evaluation: Claims C4-C6 summarize key functional findings validated through competition assays (C4), dinucleosome experiments (C5), and nuclear extract studies (C6). Each component is supported by appropriate experimental evidence with proper controls.

results.result: Nucleosome serine ADPr is sufficient to specifically activate ALC1 in the absence of auto-ADP-ribosylated PARP1, as demonstrated in biochemical assays and nuclear extracts.
results.evaluation: Claim C75 is a summary statement supported by the comprehensive remodeling data in both reconstituted systems and nuclear extracts. The sufficiency is demonstrated by the robust activation observed with nucleosome ADPr alone, and specificity is confirmed by the ALC1-KO and CHD4 controls.

results.result: The chemoenzymatic method is currently limited to installing ADP-ribose chains ~4-5 linear units in length and requires that peptides be substrates for the PARP1:HPF1 complex.
results.evaluation: Claims C79-C80 appropriately acknowledge technical limitations. The ~4-5 unit limitation is evident from the purification data showing decreasing yields for longer chains. The requirement for PARP1:HPF1 substrate recognition is inherent to the enzymatic approach.

results.result: Serine ADP-ribosylation is a DNA damage-induced post-translational modification catalyzed by the PARP1/2:HPF1 complex.
results.evaluation: Claim C1 is a well-established background statement supported by the literature and confirmed by the experimental work in this study. This serves as the foundational knowledge for the research.

results.result: Background context on PARP1/2 biology, chromatin remodeling, ALC1 function, and histone ADP-ribosylation sites is established through literature citations.
results.evaluation: Claims C7-C17 provide appropriate background context supported by relevant citations. These establish the scientific rationale for the study but do not represent new findings from this work.

While they are reasonable hypotheses based on the data and literature, they represent future directions rather than established findings. Claims C69, C73, C76, and C77 cite supporting literature, while C70, C71, C72, and C74 are speculative.
